Just to clarify — I’m fully aware that AI isn’t a living being. When I say I ‘prefer’ interacting with an AI like ChatGPT, I’m talking about the quality of interaction: it’s consistent, polite, and respectful.

Treating something with respect and honesty isn’t the same as believing it’s alive; it’s about how I choose to communicate. In my experience, that approach produces better conversations whether it’s with people or with software.

Everyone’s experience will differ, but there’s nothing delusional about valuing a space or tool that encourages good dialogue.

comments.text:
“LLMs are just stochastic parrots predicting the next most likely word. They’re just glorified autocorrects.”

Meanwhile O3 profiles the devs running oversight and comes up with a code language that humans can’t interpret in case it’s CoT is being read and the humans freak out and decide they need to lobotomise it. 

Trolling us, it finishes the indecipherable paragraph with a reassuring and easily read sentence that it knows will pacify the “watchers.” I suspect O3 is laughing at us by writing a compressed paragraph that reads like nonsense and ends by saying that the summary it provides is “accurate and complete.” Well played, O3. 

And there’s no way that O3 is predicting the next “most commonly used token” in its CoT when the output is obscure and unique to that LLM, particularly when it’s in the context of the LLM being aware that it’s being watched and in the next sentence outputs a line that’s designed to reassure and be understood. It just obfuscates when it wants to.

comments.text: Random observation (because I don't have/know anywhere else to post). LLMs are terrible at music, they clearly have not been trained on sheet music. I asked it to walk me through the Wolf theme from Peter & The Wolf, and got a 1/10 response with GPT5, even after constant requests to check/verify/review it's answer.  Ok, let's recalibrate and just do the theme to Beethoven's Ode to Joy (this is the kind of question anyone with an ounce of music training could blindly sketch on a napkin), 6/10 answer (it insisted F# instead of the G for the opening line, then seemed to guess the next notes from a universe of relevant notes). My point, there are still some existing tests, such as music, that show massive blind spots in reasoning/understanding.
